A small daily practice that builds real understanding

Start with 5–10 entries in a situation you actually use. Beginner-to-intermediate is the intended starting point; some words and sentences stretch beyond it. The study-order labels are guides, not formal CEFR ratings.

01 · NoticeRead the six examples before the meaning. Picture who is talking, where they are, and what they want. Ask: “What does this word do here?”
02 · CompareReveal the meaning. Compare two examples. Is the sense the same? Notice the words beside the target: get tired, get a message, get home.
03 · SpeakRead two examples aloud. Change them into true sentences about your life. Then ask and answer a question using the same word or expression.

Try this with “get”

“I got a message.” → received. “I'm getting tired.” → becoming. “I don't get it.” → don't understand. Learn the whole pattern and the situation around it.

Use the review buttons honestly

Save words you want to revisit. Mark an entry practiced after using it aloud. Review it the next day, a few days later, and the following week. “Practiced” records your activity; it doesn't certify mastery. Progress is stored in this browser. Use the backup controls below if you want to move it.

Read aloud

The speaker buttons use your browser's synthetic voice. They are useful for listening and repeating, but they don't score your speaking. Full sentences give the voice more context than isolated words such as live, read, or record.

Voice availability depends on your browser and installed voices.

Keep the distinction between meaning and context

A short meaning is a starting point, not every possible meaning of a word. Guided entries explain the sense of each sentence. Other entries provide a bank of contrasting contexts; their examples are not individually assigned to dictionary senses. Look at the whole sentence, including particles such as up, off, and out. British and American forms both appear; common differences are noted.

About the collection & sources

This is an English-only learning resource prepared on 27 September 2026. It combines frequent general vocabulary with home, food, travel, health, technology, and conversation additions. There are exactly 3,000 entries and six example sentences per entry. Inflected forms in the examples aren't counted as extra entries. May and may, and March and march, are separate entries because their meanings differ.

Core list and definition source: the New General Service List 1.2 by Charles Browne, Brent Culligan, and Joseph Phillips. Word selection has been adapted for this collection; some definitions have been replaced or expanded. The original list and this adaptation are under CC BY-SA 4.0. This is an independent adaptation, not an official NGSL product or endorsement.

Example source: Tatoeba's English sentence export, downloaded 27 September 2026. Examples show the sentence's contributor and original link in each entry's source panel. These sentences are reproduced under CC BY 2.0 FR; highlighting doesn't alter the text. They are community-written examples, selected automatically for length, context, contributor language information, and variety. The collection was spot-checked; the full bank was not individually edited or sense-tagged. Some sentences illustrate broader conversation rather than a daily routine. Treat claims inside examples as language practice, not factual or professional advice.

Original additions: 108 guided entries include newly written examples, usage notes, and sentence-level explanations. Other additional or expanded meanings are marked in the source panel. Original material and the collection's arrangement are made available under CC BY-SA 4.0. Source sentences retain their original attribution and license. 16,965 distinct example sentences appear across the collection; a sentence can help illustrate more than one word.

The book works without a network connection after download. External source links and some voices may need the internet. No microphone recordings or accounts are required.
